'''Ravenloft''' is the common name for the '''Demiplane of Dread''', a [[demiplane]] floating in the [[Ethereal plane]], and also the name of the [[Dungeons & Dragons]] campaign setting taking place in that demiplane. The place is run by dark powers who allow the worthy to leave, but all others are imprisoned for the rest of their lives. It's made up of chunks of various Prime worlds, pulled (or perhaps duplicated) from their original worlds, twisted into dark parodies of themselves. Whether it's an individual or a whole country, getting pulled into Ravenloft is often referred to in terms like "getting claimed by the Mists." Perhaps because of the passage through the Ethereal, one is always surrounded by impenetrable mists before finding oneself in the demiplane.<ref name="gtte46">{{b|Planescape|A Guide to the Ethereal Plane|pdf=17293|page=46}}</ref>
After the Spellplague and the transformation of the [[Demiplane of Shadow]] into the [[Shadowfell]], Ravenloft's domains shattered apart, and were drawn from the Ethereal into the new plane. Although no longer a single cohesive unit, the now-disparate [[Domains of Dread]] remain under the control of the Dark Powers.
= Demiplane of Dread =
== Personalities ==
The only known personality to have found themselves on the planes via Ravenloft is the lich [[Vecna]], who exploited a loophole in the multiverse which funneled him directly into [[Sigil]] at the exact moment that he claimed godhood.
== Portals ==
Ravenloft, like [[Carceri]], is a place of punishment for its denizens, in particular its Dark Lords. So while there may be many ways in, there are very few ways out. This even extends to the [[Border Ethereal]]. A traveler may enter the border, take a peek at the demiplane, but they will be unable to return to the [[Ethereal plane|Deep Ethereal]].<ref name="gtte16">{{b|Planescape|A Guide to the Ethereal Plane|pdf=17293|page=16}}</ref>
when Vecna "punched" his way into Sigil, his domain, Cavitius, vanished, returning into Mist. Some of those caught in the void before the Mists rushed in to fill the vacuum were likewise ejected into Sigil.<ref name="dvd121122">{{b|D&D|Die Vecna Die!|pdf=17483|page=121-122}}</ref>
== Gods ==
Ravenloft's domains are pulled from different [[Prime Material plane|Prime worlds]], so those denizens typically worship the gods native to those worlds. The inhabitants of Sithicus, for example, come from [[Krynn]], and are therefore likely to worship members of the Krynnish pantheon. A listing of all the gods worshipped within Ravenloft is beyond the scope of this Wiki.
While normally clerics within the Ethereal receive spells as though they were two levels lower, due to their increased distance from the Outer Planes, clerics in Ravenloft receive spells normally, as though they were on the Prime Material. It's rumored by some that this is because the spells are not granted by the gods, but by the inscrutable Dark Powers responsible for Ravenloft itself.

== Background Information ==
* '''Ravenloft''' is the primary setting for the ''Ravenloft'' campaign setting. * Aside from Planescape (which encompasses the entire multiverse), Ravenloft is notable for being the only campaign setting which is not set on the Prime Material Plane, and thus beyond the reach of spelljamming vessels. (Although it's been noted that the Mists can roam wildspace and can still capture a spelljammer.) * Ravenloft contains domains duplicating lands pulled from across the Prime Material, but it rarely lets anyone leave. As both a sort of planar nexus and also a cage, it's very similar to Sigil in many respects, or perhaps a inverse of Sigil. It's perhaps some aspect of this similar nature that allowed Vecna to twist the fabric of the demiplane itself into a funnel, to push past the [[Lady of Pain]]'s wards, and enter Sigil.

The '''Revolutionary League''' are a [[faction]] who believe that all the other factions just care about holding on to what they have. No one cares about the truth. They want to free everyone from the factions' chains, destroying the factions stopping everyone from finding out the real truth of the multiverse, and then rebuilding with what's left.
== History == * [[574 BFHR]]: The time of [[Fraternity of Order]] [[Factol]] [[Jaretta]]. "Anarchists" are mentioned in Guvner records during this time, who may or may not be the same group as the eventual Revolutionary League.<ref name="fm114">{{b|Planescape|The Factol's Manifesto|pdf=17275|nip=1|page=114}}</ref> * [[174 BFHR]]: An Anarchist kills the [[factol]] of the [[Mercykillers]] via a spell, then managed to pin the blame on the [[Fated]]. The following war involved almost a dozen factions and results in the destruction of three of them.<ref name="fm114">{{b|Planescape|The Factol's Manifesto|pdf=17275|nip=1|page=114}}</ref> * [[70 YFHR]]: The Anarchist [[Rechvad]] develops a magical process to change one's personality, to aid in infiltration. Unfortunately duration cannot be predicted, so Rechvad is shunned for his failure.<ref name="fw65">{{b|Planescape|Faction War (book)|alt=Faction War|pdf=17299|page=65}}</ref> * [[77 YFHR]]: [[Omar]] becomes [[factol]] of the [[Harmonium]]... and immediately tries to disband the [[faction]] and shut down the [[City Barracks]]. Omar is revealed to be an Anarchist. The Harmonium later insists they simply let him think he was in charge so he'd reveal himself. The [[Mercykillers]] execute him after a brief trial, and he becomes a hero and martyr for the Anarchists.<ref name="fm114">{{b|Planescape|The Factol's Manifesto|pdf=17275|nip=1|page=114}}</ref> * [[124 YFHR]]: [[Kiim Madbone]] is framed by the Revolutionary League for the death of two [[Mercykiller]] [[factor]]s.<ref name="fw90">{{b|Planescape|Faction War (book)|alt=Faction War|pdf=17299|page=90}}</ref>
== Philosophy ==
=== Branches === Post-Faction War, the Anarchists regrouped in [[Carceri]] to decide what to do next. After all, they'd achieved what they'd wanted: the dissolution of the factions. The majority of them decided that the next step was to return to Sigil as its new rulers.
Others decided that they were done with Sigil. But, if revolution was possible there, it was possible anywhere. They call themselves the [[Second Wave]] and have started forming cells in metropolises across the planes.<ref name="dragon31548">{{b|Dragon|Dragon Magazine 315|page=48}}</ref>
== Role ==
The Anarchists have no role in the city, unless it's part of an undercover identity. At best, one might say that their role is to ensure that none of the factions become too powerful; any faction who had noticeably increased in power would also find itself the target of far more Anarchist plots to bring it down.
The Revolutionary League has toppled factions before and they can do it again.
The [[Daughters of the Light]] are a pan-factional group whose only goal is to put an end to the Anarchists.<ref name="fw17">{{b|Planescape|Faction War (book)|alt=Faction War|pdf=17299|page=17}}</ref>
== Membership == : ''See also:'' [[List of Revolutionary League members]]
; '''[[Namer]]s'''
Namers are members of cells, typically led by a factotum, and don't know any Anarchists outside their own cell.
''Benefits'': Any Anarchist can pose as a member of any other faction without being detected, although they do not receive those faction's special abilities.
; '''[[Factotum]]s'''
Higher-ranked factotums, those deemed most trustworthy, are in cells led by factors. Those factotums in term lead their own cells full of other factotums and namers.
''Benefits'': Any factotum may learn rogue nonweapon proficiencies at normal cost. Rogues gain a +2 bonus to their scores.
''Known Factotums'': * {{NPC|Beringe|planar|male|human|fighter|13|class2=thief|level2=13|Revolutionary League|ne}}<ref name="pscs-sab66">{{b|Planescape|Planescape Campaign Setting|pdf=176267|nip=1|page=66}}, ''Sigil and Beyond''</ref><ref name="fm114">{{b|Planescape|The Factol's Manifesto|pdf=17275|nip=1|page=114}}</ref> * {{NPC|Stader|planar|female|half-elf|thief|8|Revolutionary League|116}}<ref name="fm114">{{b|Planescape|The Factol's Manifesto|pdf=17275|nip=1|page=114}}</ref>
== Background Information == * The Anarchists are not to be confused with the [[Anarch's Guild]], a sect on [[Limbo]]. * Although the faction poster from the {{b|Planescape|Planescape Campaign Setting|pdf=17267|nip=1}} contained four symbols, in a practical sense, nearly every appearance of an Anarchist symbol is the 1st or 4th variant, and the 2nd and 3rd almost never appear. Those used symbols are frequently turned upside-down to give the appearance of more symbols. * It's not known why the League has four symbols. Perhaps they're fractious enough that they couldn't decide on one, or perhaps they represent different cells, or even their ability to change who they appear to be when necessary. ** Of the four symbols, the first symbol (upside-down) appears to have been by far the most popular, with eight appearances across the line. Following that: Symbol 1, 2, 3, and 4 appeared twice each, and the upside-down versions of 2, 3, and 4 appeared once each.

{{Quote |''Rules are made to be taken advantage of.'' |From ''The Wit and Wisdom of Lord Paracs'', ruler of Ribcage.<ref name="PPO2e-p22" /> }} ==Geography== The city was located in a narrow valley in the mountain range known as the [[Vale of the Spine]]. The valley was barren and deserted and surrounded by two ridges of steep mountains that arched inwards, resembling the ribs of an enormous creature.<ref name="PPO2e-p22" /> Moving away from the city, the mountains became less steep, acquiring a more angular and cubic shape toward [[Rigus]].<ref name="Dr204-p28-31">{{Cite dragon/204/The Plane Truth Part II: A Journey to the Outlands|28-31}}</ref> The Vale extended from the edge of the Outlands spireward until near the [[River Ma'at]]<ref name="PPO2e-p22" /> and was surrounded by dusty plains.<ref name="PS-SB2e-p27">{{Cite book/Planescape Campaign Setting/Sigil and Beyond|27}}</ref>
The city occupied the entirety of the valley. All passages to the mountains were closed off, so the only way in or out of the city was through its iron gates, located on both ends of the valley.<ref name="PPO2e-p22" />
==Government== Ribcage was ruled by Lord [[Quentill Paracs]] and a council of five senators. Paracs hid his authoritarian tendencies and political ploys behind the illusion that the council could overrule his decisions, although he made sure to have a sufficient number of them held in his favor at any time through bribery and threats.<ref name="PPO2e-p22" />
==History== [[Ambran|Ambran the Seeker]], a [[half-elven]] [[paladin]] of [[Oghma]] from [[Cormyr]], was sent on a mission to explore the [[planes of existence]], according to his unpublished journal that dated from during the reign of King [[Azoun Obarskyr IV]]. Traveling with [[Glin]], a [[bariaur]] guide hired to take him from [[Sigil]] to the [[Outlands]], Ambran spent a few days in Ribcage, which both were happy to leave behind on their way to [[Automata]], where they observed the start of the [[Great Modron March]] of the 13{{th}} century [[DR]].<ref name="Dr204-p28-31" /><ref name="OotA5e-p183-184">{{Cite book/Out of the Abyss|183-184}}</ref>
==Notable Locations== * The [[Citadel (Ribcage)|Citadel]], the largest building in the city and the seat of power of the Lord and Council. It was also the location of the ''[[portal]]'' to Baator.<ref name="PPO2e-p22" /> * The [[Gymnasium of Steam]], a bathhouse built over volcanic springs on the ringward side of the city.<ref name="PPO2e-p22" />
==Inhabitants== The majority of Ribcage's population consisted of [[tiefling]]s, but also included [[human]]s and other [[humanoid]]s, [[bariaur]], [[githzerai]], and a few other races. There was a surprisingly small number of [[devil]] inhabitants, due to the council's policy of keeping them out. This policy was part of an effort to prevent the city from shifting its alignment too far into [[lawful evil]], which would incur a risk of it slipping into Baator and becoming a part of it.<ref name="PPO2e-p22" />

{{Location | image = | caption = | name = Rigus | alt spelling = | aliases = | type = [[Gate-town]] | region = The [[Outlands]] | size = | elevation = | depth = | capital = | largest city = | georefs = <ref name="APPttO-p23">{{Cite book/A Player's Primer to the Outlands|23}}</ref> | demonym = | population = 20,000 | races = [[Human]], [[tiefling]] | languages = | religion = | alignment = | socrefs = <ref name="APPttO-p23" /> | imports = | exports = | currency = | comrefs = | government = Stratocracy | rulertype = Great Generals | ruler = | head of state = | leader1 = | head of government = | leader2 = | executive = | legislature = | judiciary = | allegiances = | govrefs = <ref name="APPttO-p23" /> | established = | start event = | start date = | event1 = | date1 = | event2 = | date2 = | event3 = | date3 = | event4 = | date4 = | disestablished = | end event = | end date = | predecessor = | successor = | population1 = | popyear1 = | population2 = | popyear2 = | population3 = | popyear3 = | population4 = | popyear4 = | population5 = | popyear5 = | poptable = | ruler1 = | ruleryear1 = | ruler2 = | ruleryear2 = | ruler3 = | ruleryear3 = | ruler4 = | ruleryear4 = | ruler5 = | ruleryear5 = | rulertable = | histrefs = | usethe = | useon = | inhabitants = | locations = | organizations = | settlements = | roads = | mountains = | bodies of water = | forests = | events = | food and drink = | items = }} '''Rigus''' was a large [[gate-town]] leading to [[Acheron]] from the [[Outlands]].<ref name="APPttO-p23" /> {{Quote|''"Obey or Die" isn't just a real good idea—it's the law.''|Captain Thod Direwrack of the Mercykillers<ref name="APPttO-p23" />}}
==Description== Rigus was more of a military fortress than a town. It was built on a massive hill, divided into seven rings that rose to a pinnacle. Massive octagonal [[iron]] battlements and walls separated each ring, as well as the gate-town itself. The uppermost level was called the Crown. Entrance into Rigus was through several gates in the lowest, and largest, ring. The exterior of the lower wall was treated with a mild [[poison]] to prevent [[rust monster]]s from feeding on it.<ref name="APPttO-p23" />
===Gates=== Deep below the fortress, the gate to Acheron was located in a large chamber. The main entrance was at the bottom of a long staircase that connected the Crown to the gate. The gate itself was within an archway made from the bones of various [[bariaur]]. The gate was green-yellow in color with a stripe of black down the middle, somewhat resembling the eye of a cat. As such, it was also known as the Lion's Gate.<ref name="APPttO-p23" />
==Government== The gate-town was ruled by groups called military orders. There were roughly one hundred such groups of various size and strength. Each military order was led by a general, and the generals ruled the city. However, the true source of power in Rigus was found in the Crown. Here, the spirits of former generals remained in a state of half-life, somewhat similar to that of [[liches]]. They were the true rulers of Rigus and they gave their orders and commands to the generals of the military order, who obeyed without question.<ref name="APPttO-p23" />
==Inhabitants== The inhabitants of Rigus were primarily [[humans]] and [[tiefling]]s. Every inhabitant was given a military rank and was expected to respect the military hierarchy and obey anyone with a higher rank without hesitation. When born, an inhabitant was given the rank of citizen. This rank was also given to foreigners. Promotion was given by the Great Generals. Ranks followed a typical military structure, one could be promoted from private, sergeant, lieutenant, captain, and eventually general. Anyone who broke the law, or those taken prisoner during raids, were given the rank of slave-soldier. Disobedience was considered a high crime on par with treason and was punishable by death.<ref name="APPttO-p23" />
Visitors were not given a warm welcome. Most who came to Rigus were encouraged to conduct whatever business brought them to the gate-town as quickly as possible. They were given a special plaque made from slate, which indicated they were unfamiliar with the hierarchy and laws of Rigus. This plaque meant that a visitor was not expected to have the same unquestionable obedience as the locals, but they were expected to show respect and obey as much as possible. Disrespectful visitors often had their plaques destroyed, leaving them vulnerable to the strict laws of Rigus, and were usually then taken as a slave-soldier.<ref name="APPttO-p23" />

{{DEFAULTSORT:Ma'at, River}} {{Body of water | image = Tir fo Thuinn Map.png | caption = A map depicting the River Ma'at's path through the Outlands. | name = River Ma'at | aliases = | type = River | region = The [[Outlands]] | size = | depth = | river source = [[Semuanya's Bog]] | river mouth = | tributaries = | tributary of = | georefs = <ref name="APPttO-p31">{{Cite book/A Player's Primer to the Outlands|31}}</ref><ref name="PCS.SaB-p18">{{Cite book/Planescape Campaign Setting/Sigil and Beyond|18}}</ref> | races = [[Crocodile]]s, crocodile-like creatures | socrefs = <ref name="APPttO-p31" /><ref name="PCS.SaB-p18" /> | usethe = | useon = | inhabitants = | locations = | organizations = | settlements = | mountains = | events = | food and drink = | items = }} The '''River Ma'at''' was a wide, slow-moving body of water that twisted through much of the [[Outlands]].<ref name="APPttO-p31" /><ref name="PCS.SaB-p18" />
==Geography== The source of this river was a large lake near the center of the [[Spire]], particularly a [[divine realm]] half of it known as [[Semuanya's Bog]].<ref name="APPttO-p31" /><ref name="PCS.SaB-p18" /> It regularly overflowed at its lower banks, carving a path through the rolling hills of the plane.<ref name="PCS.SaB-p18" />
The River Ma'at mostly flowed along the seventh ring (or layer) of the Outlands, occasionally crossing through other layers.<ref name="APPttO-p31" /> It passed by the [[gate-town]]s of [[Torch (gate-town)|Torch]] and [[Ribcage]], the divine realm of [[Thoth's Estate]], and the gate-towns of [[Automata]], [[Fortitude]], and [[Excelsior]], until finally terminating at a shining salt flat.<ref name="APPttO-p31">{{Cite book/A Player's Primer to the Outlands|31}}</ref> The distance between the River Ma'at and Torch was roughly a journey of three to eighteen days.<ref>{{Cite book/A Player's Primer to the Outlands|5}}</ref>
Throughout the area of Thoth's Estate, the River Ma'at was bordered on either side by deserts and swamps.<ref>{{Cite book/On Hallowed Ground|91}}</ref> There were also a number of villages and towns that dotted its banks in this realm, inhabited largely by the [[petitioner]]s of [[Thoth]].<ref name="APPttO-p31" /><ref name="PCS.SaB-p18" />
===Flora & Fauna=== It was quite common to come across [[crocodile]]s and crocodile-like creatures living within the River Ma'at.<ref name="APPttO-p31" /><ref name="PCS.SaB-p18" />
==History== During the reign of King [[Azoun Obarskyr IV]], a [[half-elven]] [[paladin]] of [[Oghma]] from [[Cormyr]] was dispatched on a mission to explore the [[planes of existence]] beyond [[Toril]]. The paladin's name was [[Ambran|Ambran the Seeker]], and excerpts from his journal still survived to the [[Present Age]]. In volume 7, Ambran described how he hired a [[bariaur]] guide named [[Glin]] to take him from [[Sigil]] to the Outlands. Then Volume 9 told of his journey from Ribcage to Automata. Once there, he was able to witness the [[Great Modron March|Modron Parade]] before continuing on to the River Ma'at, accompanied by both Glin and [[Rialiva]], a member of the [[Doomguard]].<ref>{{Cite dragon/204/The Plane Truth Part II: A Journey to the Outlands|31}}</ref>

A '''rogue modron''' is a form of [[modron]] that has been tainted by chaos. The resulting modron is still extremely logical (and typically [[lawful neutral]]), but nonetheless too chaotic to stand among the rest of their race. Many of them choose to become adventurers.
When modrons go rogue, they lose most of their special abilities. Regardless of their previous rank, they almost always take the form of [[quadrone]]s (exceptions exist, such as [[F1ND3R|F1R]], who kept their spherical monodrone form): six foot tall cubelike bodies, a fusion of flesh and clockwork mechanical parts. Each face of their body is three feet wide, with two three-foot-long legs, two three-foot-long arms, and a pair of vestigial wings. Like quadrones, some variants eschew the wings and instead possess a second pair of arms. They begin to lose memories of their time before the fall, forgetting even their previous rank.
Rogue modrons are genderless, ageless, and typically difficult to distinguish from each other. Depending on the rogue, however, some will accumulate ornamentation, which can be used to identify them.
Rogues need an understanding of organization, so in any group they join -- an adventuring party, a faction, etc. -- they need to understand their role and "rank": who is above them, and who is below them.
Rogue modrons continue to believe in an underlying order to the multiverse, and in an effort to understand hidden rules, may reach some very tenuous connections. However, with enough exposure to the multiverse, they may "loosen up" a little.
{{quote|Does your over-exuberance in attacking these slavers have anything to do with the fact that it rained yesterday?|[[Unit 87]], a rogue modron who still doesn't quite understand human motivation}}
Rogues maintain their ability to command modrons of lesser rank, and sometimes march off with their own armies of followers.<ref name="polmec14">{{b|Planescape|Planes of Law|pdf=17272|page=14, ''Mechanus''}}</ref> That's one reason rogue modrons are occasionally hunted down by [[pentadrone]]s under the command of [[nonaton]]s.<ref name="pscsms22">{{b|Planescape|Planescape Campaign Setting|pdf=17267|page=22, ''Monstrous Supplement''}}</ref>

== Background Information == * Rogue modrons are a PC race, however they were not introduced as such until midway through the line, in the {{b|Planescape|The Planewalker's Handbook|pdf=17280}}. While most other Planescape races found their way into other game lines in later editions of Planescape, rogue modrons did not. The closest equivalent is probably the Warforged of Eberron. * Curiously, many rogue modrons who include a number in their names have the digit 8. It's likely a coincidence.

The '''Seafarer's Arch''' (also the '''Seafarer's Portal''' or '''Final Port-of-Call''') is a unique portal found in [[Sigil]]'s [[Ditch]], formed by the [[Bridge That Spans Worlds]]. The Arch is a key element in Sigil's industry, allowing the large-scale shipping of material to and from the city from various locations across the planes.
Not quite a permanent [[portal]], not quite a shifting portal, the Arch is a single portal with multiple simultaneous destinations. The destination is chosen by the gate key one uses. [[Lissandra]] the Gate-Seeker has dubbed it a "multiportal."
The desired [[gate key]] to activate the portal is placed inside a special basket attached to the ship's {{w|bowsprit}}, called a [[spritcage]]. As such, as the ship travels, the gate key is the first part of the ship to touch the portal.

A '''sect''' is an organization similar to the [[faction]]s found in [[Sigil]], however a faction is headquartered in Sigil, while a sect is not.
Titles vary per sect, but some sects still use "Factol" as a term for their leader.
The planes are large -- infinitely so -- with as many beliefs as there are people. Naturally people with similar beliefs will tend to organize together and form like-minded groups. There may well be too many sects in the planes to count.
Some former factions, banished or otherwise removed from Sigil, may become sects, and likewise, a sect may become a faction if it moves into Sigil.
* The [[Incanterium]] were once a faction, turned sect, turned faction again. * The [[Beautification League]] were once a faction, and after the [[Faction War]], became a sect known as the Rosebringers. * The [[Ring Givers]] are a sect who managed to move their headquarters into Sigil and become a full faction.
Other sects are splinter sects from existing factions. They're generally still considered to be part of the faction, although their own distinct branch.
* The [[Children of the Vine]] are a group of overly hedonistic [[Society of Sensation|Sensates]]. While the main faction looks for experiences of all kinds, the Children focus on pleasurable experiences nearly to the exclusion of all else. * The [[Mathematicians]] are a group of [[Fraternity of Order|Guvners]] who focus on unraveling the secrets of [[Mechanus]]. By their nature, their attention is focused on Mechanus and not the wider planes (or Sigil in specific), making them unsuitable for consideration as their own faction.

Its purpose and characteristics evolved as new cosmologies were formulated. Other names for this plane included '''Shadowland''', the '''Demiplane of Shadow''', the '''Shadow Deep''', and simply '''Shadow'''. It existed as sort of a counterpart to the [[Feywild]], in the sense that it was a reflection, or "echo", of the [[Prime Material Plane]]. Unlike the Feywild, it was a bleak, desolate place full of decay and death.{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|69}} {{quote|It is the toxic plane of darkness and power.
It is the hidden place that hates the light.
It is the frontier of worlds unknown.}} ==Cosmology== According to early versions of the [[Great Wheel cosmology]], the Plane of Shadow was considered only a [[demiplane]]. Demiplanes formed out of the proto-matter that ebbed and flowed about the [[Ethereal Plane]], creating a finite plane with its own Border Ethereal whenever a critical mass was achieved. The largest of these was called the Demiplane of Shadow, and was made up of both [[positive energy|positive]] and [[negative energy|negative]] energy in equal measure.{{Cite dragon/213/The Demiplane of Shadow|23}} For those traveling through the Ethereal Plane, the [[Ethereal curtain|"curtain of vaporous color"]] for the Demiplane of Shadow was the color silver. [[Wizard]]s could ''[[shadow walk]]'' directly to the edge of the Shadowfell and travelers could use this plane as a [[transitive plane]] to traverse many [[Prime Material Plane|Prime Material]] miles/kilometers very quickly. [[Cleric]]s could use the ''[[plane shift]]'' spell to travel to this plane. If any were brave enough to cross the Demiplane of Shadow, it was possible to find the borders of other planes of reality.{{Cite book/Player's Handbook 2nd edition|186}} Very little was known about the Demiplane of Shadow other than it was a dim and dismal place. In later and revised versions of the Great Wheel cosmology, such as the one following the [[Second Sundering]], the Shadowfell was considered a [[parallel plane]], or an "echo" of the Material Plane, coexisting with it along with the [[Feywild]]. [[File:Shadowfell.jpg|thumb|250px|left|''The desolate landscape of the Shadowfell.'']] ==Description== [[File:Black Rift.jpg|thumb|right|A swamp cabin beside the [[Black Rift]] in the [[Shadow Swamp]].]] The most striking and immediate impression a visitor to the Plane of Shadow experienced was the lack of color and light; no sun, moon, or stars adorned the vault of the inky black sky, and all things looked as if the color had leeched out, leaving nothing but black and white, which in the dimness were more like "dark black" and "light black". A light source only illuminated half the distance it normally would, flames and fires put out less heat, and spells that dealt with light or fire were less predictable and prone to failure, whereas shadow spells were enhanced. On the other hand, although it would not illuminate as far, any light source on the plane could be spotted at a distance of up to ten times its normal range of illumination, such was the contrast to the constant gloom, similar to a star in the night sky. Even a light source that only put out shadowy illumination, like a ''[[darkness]]'' spell or a [[lantern]] burning [[shadowlight oil]], could be seen up to five times its range of illumination. Gravity and time were the same on the Shadowfell as on the Prime, but because the Shadowfell was magically morphic (and divinely morphic in the realms of [[Shar]] and [[Mask]]) the landscape was a dark, twisted echo of what existed on the Prime. Upon entering the Plane of Shadow, the local features were usually quite similar: casting ''[[shadow walk]]'' in a forest put you in a shadow forest; casting it under water dropped you in a similar body of water, ''etc''. But from that starting point, the landscape diverged rapidly away from the familiar, and on subsequent visits from the same starting point it diverged in different ways, making mapping the Shadowfell a useless endeavor.{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 3rd edition|59}} Landmarks were usually recognizable but altered in some bizarre way: buildings might be constructed in a different style, built with different materials, at a different location, and/or in any condition from dilapidated ruins to its normal appearance, for example, or otherwise strange and distorted. Similar sites were sometimes called "shadow-analogues". Due to the ever-changing landscape, the Plane of Shadow was subject to relatively frequent but very small earthquakes (called shadow quakes) that resembled an ''[[earthquake]]'' spell in an area about two hundred feet (sixty meters) in diameter. For those on the ground, damage was equivalent to a Prime earthquake, but shadow quakes could also disrupt the ''shadow walk'' spell and dump unfortunate travelers onto the Shadowfell in the middle of the disturbance at a place very likely unknown and far from their destination.{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 3rd edition|64}} Some areas on the Plane of Shadow seemed to have an affinity with the [[Negative Energy Plane]] and life-draining [[undead]] such as [[shadow]]s, [[ghost]]s, and [[vampire]]s. These "darklands" had a minor [[Planar traits#Elemental and Energy Traits|negative-dominant]] trait and unprotected visitors immediately felt the life force being sucked from their bodies—unless they exited the darkland quickly, all that was left of them was a pile of ash. Someone with protection from negative energy could stop and admire the utter desolation in an otherwise forlorn landscape, and perhaps make the acquaintance of the truly inimical undead. Thankfully, no natural vortices opened into darklands regions, preventing the unwary from stepping through into almost certain death, and keeping the creatures that thrived there from having easy access to other planes. Material Plane locations such as desecrated burial mounds, haunted battlefields, and [[necromantic]] foci frequently had a darkland echo on the Shadowfell. Other less dangerous but quite unsettling echoes occurred in areas analogous to towns and cities in the Prime Material Plane. They were nothing more than mirages, but familiar faces and places seen through the macabre mirror of the Shadowfell could be very demoralizing. Structures might appear altered, dislocated, destroyed, or replaced entirely by something else. Mirages of the living had visages of distorted nightmares, but were still recognizable enough to give travelers a jolt of fear and revulsion. Air, water, and food existed on this plane, supporting plants, animals, and some [[humanoid]]s adapted to the shadow environment. Visitors could survive indefinitely if they were willing to endure thick, foul-smelling water, food that oozed dark blood, and a pervasive nip of cold in the air.{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 3rd edition|62}} A visitor could never feel warm, would often hear or sense the presence of things that weren't there, and could never shake the feeling of being watched. It was a constantly unsettling place. Over time, exposure to the Plane of Shadow altered living things, increasing various traits and abilities but also some vulnerabilities. Emotions and the ability to experience them seemed to fade over time for those imbued with shadowstuff.{{Cite book/Tome of Magic 3.5|109}} The morphic nature of the Shadowfell could produce strange effects, mainly in areas like the [[Black Rift]] that were especially morphic,{{Cite book/Cormyr: The Tearing of the Weave|112}} and with events that had a particular affinity with the plane, like death. For example, in the Black Rift alone, a pile of bodies caused more skeletons to appear, until there were thousands.{{Cite book/Cormyr: The Tearing of the Weave|114}} More bizarre were the strange biers upon which dead bodies spontaneously appeared, apparently drawn from wherever they rested, anywhere in existence, only to disappear after a few seconds, presumably to wherever they'd come from.{{Cite book/Cormyr: The Tearing of the Weave|116, 129, 131}} Stalactites in a cave dripped ephemeral shadowstuff, which was reabsorbed into the plane rather than form a puddle. Even common mushrooms bore realistic humanoid faces, capable of twitching or blinking.{{Cite book/Cormyr: The Tearing of the Weave|115, 125}} More significantly, forests of grasping tendrils sprouted from some surfaces and reached for passersby, similar to the ''[[black tentacles]]'' spell. ===Phenomena=== [[File:Shadowfellsummoning.png|thumb|273x273px|A creature of the Shadowfell summoned to the mortal realm.]] Known as "[[shadowstuff]]",{{Cite book/Drizzt Do'Urden's Guide to the Underdark|110-111}} the material of the Shadowfell could be manipulated by [[illusionist]]s to form semi-real monsters{{Cite book/Player's Handbook 2nd edition|162}} and quasi-real [[evocation]]s{{Cite book/Player's Handbook 2nd edition|171}} that were still effective (to a lesser degree) even if the target successfully disbelieved the illusion. Another tool of illusionists was the ''[[shadow well]]'' spell, which could turn a creature's shadow into a temporary gateway into the Shadowfell. If successful, the victim was sucked into the Shadowfell through his or her shadow and spent a few moments in a pocket realm (a very tiny [[demiplane]] attached to the Shadowfell) being terrorized by dark phantasms. No physical harm resulted from this spell, but mental and emotional trauma resulting in a fear response was possible.{{Cite book/Anauroch: The Empire of Shade|144}} An unsuccessful attempt to build a gate to the Shadowfell could result in what was termed a [[failed Shadow Gate]]. A being that stepped through one was taken only momentarily to the Plane of Shadow, but in that moment a "seed of shadow" was implanted in their flesh. This could cause their flesh to be subsumed by shadow, and they would see it mist away into darkness. Many died, reduced to bare skeletons, but those who survived acquired the powers of a [[dark creature]].{{Cite book/Cormyr: The Tearing of the Weave|154}} ==History== The earliest known conscious interaction of the peoples of [[Toril]] with the Plane of Shadow was in the time of the [[Imaskari]] empire. In the Late period, ''circa'' {{Yearlink|-3500}}, the archwizard [[Madryoch the Ebon Flame]] was focused on researching the secrets of the Shadowfell and plotted to use its dark power to overthrow Lord Artificer [[Omanond]]. His plans were thwarted by a young adept named [[Hilather]].{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|18}} Knowledge of the existence of the Plane of Shadow was presumably lost with the fall of the Imaskari empire because it was some three thousand years later, in the [[-533 DR|Year of Plentiful Wine, −533 DR]], that the [[Netherese]] rediscovered it and began their study.{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Setting 3rd edition|268}} In [[1235 DR]], the [[Black Horde]] attacked Faerûn. The Horde defeated [[Eldrith the Betrayer]], who would go on to betray [[Baldur's Gate]]. They killed her and she was reborn out of hatred. In her soul of hatred, the [[Onyx Tower]] was created and tied to her life. The [[Onyx Heart]] was located in the Plane of Shadow and only with its destruction could the Onyx Tower be destroyed.{{Cite game/Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance}} An [[Drogan Droganson's pupil|adventurer]] and their companions were exploring the ruined [[Netherese]] city of [[Undrentide]] in the [[1372 DR|Year of Wild Magic, 1372 DR]]. In an [[Arcanist's Tower]], they slipped through portals into its dark reflection on the Shadowfell, where they encountered [[shade]]s. The adventurer later escaped impending doom by traveling back to the Plane of Shadow using a magic mirror.{{Cite game/Neverwinter Nights: Shadows of Undrentide}} Although the souls of the dead did not begin to be drawn to the Shadow Plane until after the [[Spellplague]] and [[Shar]] transformed it into the Shadowfell,{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|65}} it was possible to trap a soul there. Notably, this happened to a king of [[Damara]], [[Gareth Dragonsbane]], in the [[1373 DR|Year of Rogue Dragons, 1373 DR]], by a cabal of wizards allied to the [[lich]] [[Sammaster]]. King Gareth's soul was rescued in the following year by a phalanx of [[paladin]]s led by the [[smoke drake]] [[Capnolithyl|Brimstone]].{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|154}} In the [[1374 DR|Year of Lightning Storms, 1374 DR]], [[Shar]]ran and [[Cyric]]ist cultists based in the [[Shadow Swamp]] on the Plane of Shadow, plotted to tear apart the [[Weave]] from the [[Black Rift]]. Adventurers pursued them through the [[Dusk Lord's Passage]] to the Shadow Swamp and disrupted their efforts, and found the [[Black Chronology]] among their detritus.{{Cite book/Cormyr: The Tearing of the Weave|72-147}} That same year, a rift to the Shadowfell was opened in the skies over [[Sembia]] and the city of [[Ordulin]] was destroyed when a shadowy tract of land fell on it.{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|157}} In [[1376 DR]], eight brave heroes ventured into the Plane of Shadow and defeated one of its guardians, [[Mordoc SeLanmere]], and destroyed the [[Onyx Heart]].{{Cite game/Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance II}} A major change afflicted the Plane of Shadow in [[1385 DR]] when [[Shar]], having successfully arranged [[Mystra]]'s death, bound the energies of the [[Negative Energy Plane]] with the plane. Since then, the plane became known as the Shadowfell, existing as a center of Shar's power as well as a transitory place for dead mortals on their way towards judgment on the [[Fugue Plane]].{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|65}} After the [[Second Sundering]], the Shadowfell no longer was a waypoint for the souls of the dead on their way to the Fugue plane, but it remained known as the Shadowfell for most people.{{Cite book/Sword Coast Adventurer's Guide|20}} ==Rumors and Legends== The special and unique nature of this plane caused not only cosmologists to speculate about its origins, but visitors and planar travelers as well. Some believed the Plane of Shadow had spontaneously formed as a [[demiplane]] out of the [[Ethereal Plane]]. However, most cosmologists and planewalkers with a sense of adventure liked to talk about the legend of the Shining Citadel. Briefly, the legend postulated that the Plane of Shadow was once bright and colorful like the Material Plane, but at some point in the distant past a mysterious group who worshiped the plane's creator took all of the light, color, and most of the life-force from the rest of the plane and concentrated it into a mighty citadel. One would think that a structure containing most of the energy from an entire [[plane of existence]] would be hard to miss, but no one has ever found the Shining Citadel, except perhaps, as the legend states, those who venture into the deepest parts of the Plane of Shadows and never return. A theory bandied about among sages stated that the [[Underdark]] was bottomless because it eventually became the Plane of Shadow. The only evidence supporting this hypothesis was that permanent ''portals'' to the Shadowfell were increasingly common the deeper one delved.{{Cite book/Underdark|120}} ==Notable Locations== [[File:ShadowfellExplorers.jpg|thumb|right|250px|''Exploring the Shadowfell.'']] ; [[Chaulssin]] :Located almost ten miles (sixteen kilometers) below the surface of [[northwest Faerûn]], beneath the northernmost peak of the [[Rauvin Mountains]],{{Cite web enhancement/City of Wyrmshadows|1}} this was originally a [[drow]] city that was captured by [[shadow dragon]]s in the [[-221 DR|Year of Shambling Shadows, −221 DR]]. Under the influence of shadow dragons for hundreds of years, the city was slowly absorbed by the Plane of Shadow{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|53}} until their overthrow in the [[634 DR|Year of the Darkspawn, 634 DR]].{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|93}} Abandoned in the [[734 DR|Year of the Splendid Stag, 734 DR]],{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|101}} the fringe of the Shadowfell continued to ebb and flow through streets and buildings filled with dangerous shadow creatures.{{Cite web enhancement/City of Wyrmshadows|2}} Chaulssin was reestablished in the [[1136 DR|Year of the Shadowkin Return, 1136 DR]], by [[Jaezred Chaulssin|House Jaezred]] as a base for the shadow dragon–blooded drow assassins.{{Cite web enhancement/City of Wyrmshadows|3}}{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|119}} ; [[Chaul'mur'ssin]] :This city was established on the Plane of Shadow by the inhabitants of Chaulssin after fleeing an advancing army from [[Menzoberranzan]] in 734 DR. The Chaulssinyr hastily traveled through dangerous caverns until they found the abandoned lairs of their shadow dragon progenitors and claimed them, eking out an existence. Eventually the city thrived and became a power that demanded respect. ;[[Evernight]] :The dismal reflection of [[Neverwinter]].{{Cite book/Neverwinter Campaign Setting|202}} It was believed to be the dark version of least one city in every world in the [[Prime Material plane]]. ;[[Gloomwrought]] :The dark twin to [[Thultanthar]] (the Shade Enclave). ; [[Mulsantir]] :Travel between the Shadowfell and the Prime Material Plane was possible in certain places in [[Mulsantir]] at certain times of day. Shadow Mulsantir contained a Temple of [[Myrkul]], in the place where a Shrine to [[Kelemvor]] stood on the Prime. Within this temple was found a portal leading to Kelemvor's domain, the [[Fugue Plane]].{{Cite game/Neverwinter Nights 2: Mask of the Betrayer}} ;[[Shadow Swamp]] :The [[Vast Swamp]] between [[Cormyr]] and [[Sembia]] had a Shadowfell counterpart, called the [[Shadow Swamp]]. Although the environment was similar in many ways, it was a great black swamp, where the water was dark and still and only moved sluggishly through the channels. Nevertheless, the landscape was different; there seemed to be more water than in the fast-growing Vast Swamp. Sites in the Vast Swamp had echoes here: the [[Lost Refuge]] in the material world had a counterpart in the so-called [[Shadow Citadel]], which followed the same plan but was even more ruined. A ''portal'' called the [[Dusk Lord's Passage]] linked the two. On the other hand, a flooded fissure that formed an ordinary lakebed in the Vast Swamp was reflected in an empty canyon in the Shadow Swamp, known as the [[Black Rift]]. Swamp water flowed in on all sides, yet the water at the bottom never rose and never seemed to drain out, an entirely unexplained phenomena of the plane. The Black Rift was especially morphic—although it remained more-or-less the same shape overall, local changes in terrain were extreme and bizarre. The interplay between the magical [[Weave]] and the [[Shadow Weave]] was especially malleable, a trait which attracted the followers of Shar. ;[[Sphur Upra]] :Located nine miles (over fourteen kilometers) below the surface of [[east Faerûn]], between the surface nations of [[Mulhorand]] and [[Murghôm]],{{Cite book/Underdark|177}} this city was established on the Shadowfell in {{Yearlink|-2954}} by five [[gloaming]] families seeking security and community. After almost 3,500 years, they expanded their city by creating ''portals'' to the [[Prime Material Plane|Material Plane]] in the [[534 DR|Year of the Spitting Viper, 534 DR]], and became a major trading post for goods between the two planes.{{Cite book/Underdark|178}} ;[[Thultanthar]] ([[City of Shade]]) :This floating enclave of [[Netherese]] origin entered the Plane of Shadow just before [[Karsus's Folly]] brought down the empire in [[-339 DR|Year of Sundered Webs, −339 DR]].{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|47}} Over the centuries, its population acclimated to the new environment and became known as [[shade]]s. In the [[1372 DR|Year of Wild Magic, 1372 DR]], Thultanthar was brought back to the Material Plane and became known as the City of Shade.{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Setting 3rd edition|280}}{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|152}} The inhabitants then began the rebuilding of the Netherese empire.{{Cite book/Lords of Darkness|78}} ===Realms=== Only three [[deities]] were known to have claimed the Plane of Shadow as their home: *[[Mask]], the Master of all Thieves and Lord of Shadows had a realm on this plane called [[Shadow Keep]]. It was made out of shadowstuff and was extremely difficult to see even when standing right next to it. *[[Shar]], Mistress of the Night and Lady of Loss, once resided in a high tower called the [[Palace of Loss]]. It had no apparent means of entry or exit, but her followers had no trouble gaining access. She sometimes kept prisoners there so she could enjoy their suffering. After the [[Spellplague]], she moved her abode to the [[Towers of Night]] and left behind a deep dark hole guarded by evil creatures. This [[Foundation of Loss]] exuded palpable grief and was reported to contain a portal to her home in the Towers of Night. *[[Null]], [[Draconic pantheon|draconic god]] of death, had realms named the [[Mausoleum of Chronepsis]] and the [[Mausoleum of Pain]] in the [[Outlands]] and [[Carceri]], respectively. Parts of these were thought to exist on the Plane of Shadow at the same time.{{Cite book/Cult of the Dragon|121}} ===Domains of Dread=== [[File:Gates_of_barovia.jpg|thumb|230px|''The gates of Barovia, one of the Domains of Dread.'']] {{Main|Domains of Dread}} In remote corners of the Shadowfell there were [[demiplane]]s created by the [[Dark Powers]] which served as prisons to trap creatures of extreme evil to serve as sustenance. One such demiplane was the valley of [[Barovia]], ruled by the [[vampire]] [[Strahd von Zarovich]], himself a prisoner of the Dark Powers.{{Cite book/Dungeon Master's Guide 5th edition|51}} Passages to Barovia were rumored to exist somewhere in the [[Misty Forest]], based on reports of [[werewolf]] attacks and [[Vistani]] presence in [[Daggerford]] and surrounding areas.{{Cite book/Curse of Strahd|19-22}} [[Elminster |Elminster, the Sage of Shadowdale]], had shown himself aware of count Strahd and his mist-filled domain, as well as how to journey to-and-from there somewhat freely. He briefly sent [[volo|Volothamp Gaddarm]] to Barovia to explore the valley, although Volo was initially unaware of the dangers.{{Cite dragon+/6/Travel Talk: Volo's Visit to Barovia}} ==Inhabitants== [[File:Shadowfell-shadar-kai-5e.jpg|thumb|left|250px|''The [[shadar-kai]], denizens of the Shadowfell.'']] The Shadowfell was home to a mysterious form of [[undead]] called [[shadow]]s,{{Cite book/Lords of Darkness 1st edition|32-33}} other "shadow" creatures such as the [[shadow mastiff]]{{Cite book/Monster Manual II (1983)|84}} and [[shadow dragon]],{{Cite book/Monster Manual II (1983)|58-59}} and a race of [[humanoid]]s known as [[shade]]s.{{Cite book/Monster Manual II (1983)|108}} In addition to those, there were numerous other inhabitants, such as communities of [[shadar-kai]], [[Shadovar]], and [[dark one]]s. Probably the most dominant race of beings on the Plane of Shadow were the shades—ancestors of ancient [[Netherese]] [[human]]s who resided on the plane in their floating city for centuries and acquired many abilities from immersion in shadow essence.{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Setting 3rd edition|314-315}} [[Malaugrym]]s may have been superior to shades, having the advantage of being [[shapeshifter]]s and practically immortal unless killed in some fashion; but their small numbers, fierce independence, and difficulty in mastering interplanar travel made them much less organized and effective.{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Setting 3rd edition|277}}The ''[[Player's Guide to Faerûn]]'' states on page 165 that the malaugryms are actually native to a small [[demiplane]] attached to the Plane of Shadow. Other creatures that were either native to the plane or attracted to it included [[bodak]]s, [[cloaker]]s, [[darkweaver]]s,{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn|163}} [[ephemera]] of all kinds,{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 3rd edition|169-172}} [[veserab]]s,{{Cite book/Anauroch: The Empire of Shade|156}} [[lich]]es, [[nightshade]]s,{{Cite book/Monster Manual 3.5|195}} [[shadar-kai]], [[shadurakul]], [[spectre]]s, and [[wraith]]s. Occasionally, animals and monsters would wander or fall into a vortex to the Shadowfell and become trapped there. Those that survived eventually took on shadow-given abilities, carved out a niche in the ecosystem, and preyed on whatever attracted their attention. Examples included [[ape]]s, [[basilisk]]s, [[bear]]s, [[owlbear]]s, [[rat]]s, [[umber hulk]]s, and [[wolves]]. Such creatures could give rise to [[dark creature]]s, shadowy counterparts of natural creatures.{{Cite book/Tome of Magic 3.5|158-161}}{{Cite book/Cormyr: The Tearing of the Weave|152}} [[Shadow demon]]s also inhabited this plane. These [[fiend]]s were responsible for the creation of the race known as [[krinth]], having interbred with [[Netherese]] slaves.{{Cite book/Anauroch: The Empire of Shade|150}} [[Shadow sea serpent]]s were not native to the Plane of Shadow but were bred there by the Shadovar, crossing warm-blooded carnivorous orcas with vile shadow creatures. These serpents hunted in packs both in the sea and on land.{{Cite book/Anauroch: The Empire of Shade|151-152}} Especially during the period between the [[Spellplague]] and the [[Second Sundering]], the Shadowfell became also prominently populated with dead creatures such as [[ghost]]s, [[specter]]s, and other [[undead]] who for whatever reason refused to leave the Shadowfell and continue on to the [[Fugue Plane]]. ===Notable Inhabitants === *[[Ambergris (person)|Ambergris]], [[dwarf]] [[Shadovar]] [[cleric]] of [[Dumathoin]] and former member of [[Cavus Dun]].{{Cite book/The Last Threshold}} *[[Afafrenfere]], human Shadovar [[monk]], former member of Cavus Dun, former member of [[Brothers of the Gray Mists]], and former member of the [[Monastery of the Yellow Rose]]. *[[Dark Powers]], vestiges of ancient dead [[evil]] [[god]]s that either dwell on the plane or were banished there, and feed on evil creatures that become trapped in the Shadowfell.{{Cite book/Curse of Strahd|181}} *[[Drasek Riven]], a godling, had his fortress here, where he hid from [[Rivalen|Rivalen the Nightseer]] and the archdevil [[Mephistopheles]], both of whom shared a piece of the divine essence Drasek himself had.{{Cite book/Shadowrealm}} *[[Draygo Quick]], a [[Netherese]] lord and powerful [[warlock]].{{Cite book/The Companions|29}} * [[Effron|Effron the Twisted]], [[tiefling]] Shadovar warlock, and former student of Draygo Quick. *[[The Ghost King]], a composite being formed from: [[Hephaestus]] a [[dracolich]]; [[Crenshinibon]] and its seven disembodied [[lich]]es; and the sentience of [[Yharaskrik]], an [[illithid]]; which had powers over the undead denizens of the Shadowfell. *[[Glorfathel]], [[elf]] Shadovar [[wizard]] and member of Cavus Dun. *[[Herzgo Alegni]], tiefling Shadovar warlord, who wielded [[Charon's Claw (sword)|Charon's Claw]]. *[[Jermander]], a tiefling Shadovar [[warrior]] and member of Cavus Dun. *[[Parbid]], tiefling Shadovar monk, member of Cavus Dun, and the [[Brothers of the Gray Mists]]. *[[Parise Ulfbinder]], a Netherese lord. *[[Ratsis|Ratsis the Spider Farmer]], a human male [[shade]] and member of Cavus Dun. *The [[Raven Queen]] had a divine realm known as the [[Fortress of Memories]] here.{{Cite book/Mordenkainen's Tome of Foes|58-59}} ==Appendix== ===Appearances=== :;Novels: ::''[[Charon's Claw (novel)|Charon's Claw]]'' • ''[[The Companions]]'' • ''[[The Ghost King]]'' • ''[[The Last Threshold]]'' • ''[[The Shadow Stone]]'' ::{{Refonly}} ::''[[The Siege]]'' :;Adventures ::''[[Cormyr: The Tearing of the Weave]]'' :;Video games :: [[Baldur's Gate series]] (''[[Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance]]'', ''[[Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance II]]'') • [[Neverwinter Nights series]] (''[[Neverwinter Nights: Shadows of Undrentide]]'', ''[[Neverwinter Nights 2: Mask of the Betrayer]]'') ::{{Refonly}} ::''[[Dungeons & Dragons Online]]: [[Dungeons & dragons online/The Shadowfell Conspiracy|The Shadowfell Conspiracy]]'' :;Fiction ::''[[Travel Talk: Volo's visit to Barovia]]'' ===Gallery=== Neverwinter Nights 2 - Plane of Shadow 4.png|A part of the village of [[Mulsantir]] in the Shadow Plane in ''Neverwinter Nights 2: Mask of the Betrayer''.
